title: Structuring Presentations and Writing Executive Summaries
summary: Learn to structure a short presentation as opening, body, and call to action, and to write an executive summary with a takeaway title and section headers.

steps.title: Opening, Body, Call to Action
steps.lede: With the Lagos finding, the recommendation, and a simplified chart ready, the last piece is putting them in an order that carries the operations manager from 'why am I reading this' to 'what do you want me to do.'

blocks.text: A summary should have an obvious beginning, middle, and end. In the beginning, level-set the audience; in the middle, present the analysis; in the end, conclude with the key takeaways. In a story's structure, the beginning establishes the context of the situation, and this gets carried onward to the twist, before the ending brings the story to its close. Mapped onto the Lagos presentation: the beginning is the situation (delivery times across the three cities this month), the twist is the Lagos slowdown, and the ending is the courier recommendation.

blocks.title: Three-Part Presentation Spine

nodes.label: Opening
nodes.detail: Context / situation — why are we reviewing Lagos delivery times?

nodes.label: Body
nodes.detail: Finding + evidence — Lagos avg delivery time rose from 22 to 30 min; distance is the strongest driver.

nodes.label: Call to Action
nodes.detail: What is being asked — approve adding one courier on the longest Lagos routes.

blocks.alt_text: Three-part presentation spine: Opening (context/situation) → Body (finding + evidence) → Call to Action (what is being asked), with the Lagos delivery example mapped onto each slot.

steps.title: Ending with a Call to Action
steps.lede: The presentation closes by asking the audience for something — once they have the context to understand the request.

blocks.text: A presentation can end with a call to action, stating what is being asked of the audience, once the audience has the context needed to understand the request — so the Lagos presentation can open with why the review happened, move through the finding and chart, and close by asking management to approve one added courier.

steps.title: Beginning, Middle, End
steps.lede: Three slides from the Lagos presentation are shown out of order. Which order places them correctly in the opening–body–call-to-action structure?

public.prompt: Three slides from the Lagos presentation are shown out of order. Which order places them correctly into opening–body–call to action?

options.text: Slide A (context/situation) → Slide B (finding + evidence) → Slide C (call to action)
Slide B (finding + evidence) → Slide A (context/situation) → Slide C (call to action)
Slide C (call to action) → Slide A (context/situation) → Slide B (finding + evidence)
Slide A (context/situation) → Slide C (call to action) → Slide B (finding + evidence)

opt_context_finding_action.message: Correct. A presentation should have an obvious beginning (context/situation), middle (finding + evidence), and end (call to action).

opt_finding_context_action.message: Not quite. The beginning should establish the context of the situation before presenting findings. Starting with findings leaves the audience without necessary background.

opt_action_context_finding.message: Not quite. The call to action should come at the end, after the context and findings have been established. Starting with the request leaves the audience unprepared.

opt_context_action_finding.message: Not quite. The call to action should come at the end, after the findings have been presented. Placing it before the findings means the audience has not yet seen the evidence supporting the request.

correct.message: Right. The structure is opening (context), body (finding + evidence), and call to action (what is being asked).

incorrect.message: Remember the three-part structure: beginning (context), middle (finding + evidence), end (call to action).

hints: The beginning should establish the context before presenting findings.
The call to action comes at the end, after the evidence has been presented.

steps.title: Arrange the Lagos Presentation
steps.lede: Drag the five Lagos presentation elements into the correct opening–body–call-to-action order.

public.prompt: Drag the five Lagos presentation elements into the correct opening–body–call-to-action order.

items.text: QuickShip's Lagos operations have grown 40% in the past year
40% of deliveries now exceed the 60-minute target
Eastern districts average 78 minutes, 18 minutes over target
A second hub in the eastern zone would reduce average delivery time to 42 minutes
We recommend approving the second hub by end of quarter

correct.message: Perfect. You organized the elements into the correct structure: opening (context + problem), body (evidence + solution), and call to action (request).

incorrect.message: Think about the three-part structure. The opening establishes context, the body presents findings and evidence, and the end states what is being asked.

hints: Start with context to establish the situation.
Present the problem and evidence in the middle.
End with the solution and what you are asking for.

steps.title: The Executive Summary: One Page That Must Stand Alone
steps.lede: The full Lagos delivery-time presentation may never get read past its first page.

blocks.text: An executive summary is a one- or two-page overview of a much longer presentation, provided so the reader gets the main messages without reading the entire communication; it may be the only thing the audience ever looks at. The summary's title should state the main takeaway and set the tone for the rest of the page, and the summary should follow a narrative arc with an obvious beginning, middle, and end — a title like 'Lagos delivery times are slowing — recommend adding one courier' already tells a skimming reader the point before they read a word of the body.

Content should be grouped into easily-discernible sections with text headers, so someone scanning for only a few seconds still understands the main points. Bullets should generally be avoided in favour of well-constructed sentences and mini-paragraphs, except when listing elements. A short 'Finding' section and a short 'Recommendation' section, each a sentence or two, serve a scanning reader better than a single unbroken paragraph.

before.title: Before: unstructured paragraph

nodes.label: Single unbroken paragraph: 'Lagos delivery times rose from 22 to 30 minutes in Month 2. Distance is the strongest driver (r=0.82). We recommend adding one courier on the longest routes. Traffic patterns and order volume were ruled out as primary causes. The analysis covered 20 orders across Lagos, Abuja, and Kano.'

before.alt_text: Before: one unbroken paragraph with no title, no section headers, mixing finding, recommendation, and method.

after.title: After: structured executive summary

nodes.label: Title: Lagos delivery times are slowing — recommend adding one courier
Finding: Lagos average delivery time rose from 22 to 30 minutes in Month 2. Distance is the strongest driver of delivery time (r = 0.82).
Recommendation: Add one courier on the longest Lagos routes to bring average delivery time back below 25 minutes.

after.alt_text: After: executive summary with a takeaway title, a Finding section header, and a Recommendation section header — each a sentence or two of prose.

blocks.change_summary: Headers and a takeaway title replace the undifferentiated paragraph, letting a scanning reader find the finding and recommendation in seconds.

steps.title: What Makes a Good Executive Summary?
steps.lede: Four executive summary drafts are shown. Which one best follows the taught structure?

public.prompt: Four executive summary drafts are shown. Which one best follows the taught structure?

options.text: Draft A: Has a takeaway title, uses section headers ('Finding' and 'Recommendation'), and presents content in prose paragraphs
Draft B: Has a descriptive title, uses bullet points throughout, and covers findings and recommendations
Draft C: Has a takeaway title and prose paragraphs, but no section headers to distinguish findings from recommendations
Draft D: Has section headers and prose, but runs to four pages with extensive detail

opt_structured.message: Correct. An executive summary should have a takeaway title, section headers to group content into easily-discernible sections, and prose paragraphs rather than bullets.

opt_bullets.message: Not quite. While bullet points are common, the taught structure uses prose paragraphs with section headers. Bullets can make the summary feel like a list rather than a narrative.

opt_no_headers.message: Not quite. Section headers are important for grouping content into easily-discernible sections. Without them, the reader has to work harder to distinguish findings from recommendations.

opt_long.message: Not quite. An executive summary should be a one- or two-page overview, not four pages. The goal is to provide a concise summary, not extensive detail.

correct.message: Right. The executive summary structure includes a takeaway title, section headers, and prose paragraphs — all within one or two pages.

incorrect.message: Remember the key elements: a takeaway title, section headers to group content, prose paragraphs, and a one- or two-page length.

hints: Section headers help the reader quickly identify findings and recommendations.
Prose paragraphs create a narrative arc rather than a list.
An executive summary should be concise — one or two pages.

steps.title: Write an Executive Summary
steps.lede: Using the Lagos scenario below, write a three-sentence executive summary with a title stating the main takeaway, a sentence covering the finding, and a sentence stating the recommendation — in prose, not bullets.

public.instruction:
Using the Lagos scenario below, write a three-sentence executive summary with a title stating the main takeaway, a 'Finding' section, and a 'Recommendation' section. Your summary should:
• Have a title that states the main takeaway
• Include a 'Finding' section header followed by one sentence describing the delivery-time problem
• Include a 'Recommendation' section header followed by one sentence proposing the second hub
• Use prose (not bullets)
• Be concise (approximately 50–75 words total)

rubric.criterion: Title states main takeaway (e.g., 'Second Lagos Hub Needed to Meet Delivery Targets')
Includes a 'Finding' section header followed by a sentence describing the delivery-time problem
Includes a 'Recommendation' section header followed by a sentence proposing the second hub
Uses prose paragraphs rather than bullet points
The summary is concise (approximately 50–75 words) and focused on the key points

correct.message: Excellent work. Your executive summary follows the taught structure with a takeaway title, section headers, and prose paragraphs.

incorrect.message: Review the structure: a takeaway title, 'Finding' and 'Recommendation' section headers, and prose paragraphs (not bullets).

hints: Start with a title that states the main takeaway, not just a description.
Use section headers ('Finding' and 'Recommendation') to organize your content.
Write in prose paragraphs, not bullet points.
Keep it concise — aim for 50–75 words total.

steps.title: Presentation Structure and Executive Summaries — Key Takeaways
steps.lede: What you practised in this tile.

blocks.text: Structure every presentation as opening (context), body (finding + evidence), and call to action (what you are asking). An executive summary is a one- or two-page overview that may be the only thing the audience reads; its title should state the main takeaway, and content should be grouped under section headers in prose, not bullets.

remediation_steps.title: Opening, Body, Call to Action — The Three Slots
remediation_steps.lede: Every presentation has three jobs to do, in order.

blocks.text: The opening level-sets the audience: why are we looking at Lagos delivery times? The body presents the finding and the evidence: delivery times rose from 22 to 30 minutes in Month 2, and distance is the strongest driver. The call to action closes the presentation by stating what is being asked — approve adding one courier — only after the audience has the context needed to understand the request. Placing the call to action before the context leaves the audience without the 'why', making the request harder to evaluate.
